title: Who Owns the Past?
subtitle: Museums in Europe and North America are under mounting pressure to return objects acquired in the colonial era. The arguments on both sides deserve closer scrutiny than they usually receive.

paragraphs.text: In February 1897 a British military force entered Benin City, in what is now southern Nigeria, in reprisal for the killing of a British-led delegation some weeks earlier. The city was burned and the royal palace stripped of thousands of objects: cast brass plaques that had once adorned the palace, commemorative heads, carved ivory tusks. Many were auctioned to defray the costs of the expedition, and within a few years the so-called Benin Bronzes were dispersed among the museums and private collections of Europe and North America. For most of the following century they were admired as masterpieces of African art, yet the circumstances of their removal attracted remarkably little comment in the institutions that displayed them.

That indifference has now largely evaporated. In 2018 a report commissioned by the French president recommended that cultural objects removed from Africa without consent should be restituted, and France has since returned twenty-six treasures to the Republic of Benin. In 2022 Germany transferred ownership of more than a thousand Benin Bronzes to Nigeria, and universities and smaller museums in Britain and the United States have made similar gestures. What was, a generation ago, a marginal demand pressed by a handful of governments has become a mainstream expectation, and curators who once regarded the matter as closed now find themselves obliged to defend not merely individual acquisitions but the very rationale of their collections.

The most familiar defence of the status quo rests on the notion of the 'universal museum'. In 2002 the directors of some of the world's largest museums signed a declaration asserting that their institutions served 'not just the citizens of one nation but the people of every nation', and that objects acquired in earlier times had to be viewed in the light of the values of that earlier era. On this view, a sculpture displayed in London or Berlin alongside the art of many other civilisations acquires a significance it could never possess in isolation. The argument is not without force. Encyclopaedic collections do permit comparisons that illuminate human creativity as a whole, and a great many objects entered them through purchase, exchange or gift rather than plunder.

Yet the universalist case is weaker than its proponents tend to concede. For one thing, the 'universal' public it invokes is in practice concentrated in a few affluent cities, to which many descendants of the objects' makers cannot easily obtain visas, let alone afford the journey - a difficulty that defenders of the universal museum seldom address. For another, the claim that past acquisitions should be judged by past standards raises the awkward question of whose standards are meant. The sacking of Benin City was deplored by some observers even at the time; its inhabitants did not consent to it. To treat the values of the victorious party as the values of the era is to mistake power for consensus.

The Parthenon sculptures in the British Museum illustrate how much more intractable the issue becomes when legality, rather than outright violence, is in dispute. They were removed from the Acropolis in Athens in the early 1800s by agents of Lord Elgin, the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire, which then ruled Greece, and were purchased from him by the British government in 1816. The museum maintains that Elgin acted with the permission of the Ottoman authorities; critics counter that the original document has never been found, and that the consent of an occupying power is a dubious foundation for ownership. Greece has formally sought the sculptures' return since the 1980s. The British Museum is prevented by an Act of Parliament from disposing of items in its collection except in narrowly defined circumstances, and has floated the idea of a long-term loan - a proposal Greece has resisted, since accepting it would imply recognising British ownership.

Opponents of restitution raise two further objections. The first is the spectre of a slippery slope: if one object goes, the argument runs, the great collections will eventually be emptied. Experience thus far suggests otherwise. Claims have been specific and selective, and the museums that have returned objects remain amply stocked. The second objection, that countries of origin lack the means to conserve what they receive, deserves to be taken more seriously, but it is too often voiced in a tone reminiscent of the paternalism of the colonial era itself. When Nigeria's government decreed in 2023 that returned bronzes would belong to the Oba of Benin, the kingdom's traditional ruler, some European commentators asked whether the objects would remain accessible to the public. It is a legitimate question, but it is one for Nigerians to answer: the right to make decisions about one's own heritage cannot be made conditional on making the decisions that former colonial powers would prefer.

None of this implies that every object acquired abroad should be sent back, or that a transfer of ownership resolves every difficulty. Objects bought openly differ from those taken at gunpoint, and many cases lie somewhere in between. Nor are digital replicas, however faithful, an adequate substitute: a scan cannot carry the meaning that the original holds for a community whose history it embodies. What is required is a willingness to examine the history of each collection honestly and to accept that, where force or coercion is clearly established, the burden of proof should rest with the institution that wishes to retain an object rather than with those who want it back. Museums that embrace this principle may find that they lose fewer treasures than they fear - and gain a credibility that no masterpiece can confer.

items.statement: Throughout the twentieth century, museums holding the Benin Bronzes paid close attention to how the objects had been obtained.
items.evidence: the circumstances of their removal attracted remarkably little comment in the institutions that displayed them
items.note: The writer says the museums paid very little attention to how the objects were removed.

items.statement: Large collections that bring together objects from many cultures can reveal things that a single culture's objects cannot.
items.evidence: Encyclopaedic collections do permit comparisons that illuminate human creativity as a whole

items.statement: Supporters of the universal museum overlook the obstacles that prevent many people from visiting the museums concerned.
items.evidence: cannot easily obtain visas, let alone afford the journey - a difficulty that defenders of the universal museum seldom address

items.statement: A long-term loan of the Parthenon sculptures would be a sensible way of settling the dispute.
items.note: The writer reports the British Museum's loan idea and Greece's reason for resisting it, but does not say whether the writer thinks it would be a good solution.

items.statement: Returning some objects is likely to lead eventually to the emptying of major museums.
items.note: The writer presents the 'slippery slope' fear as the opponents' argument and then rejects it.

items.statement: Museums in Nigeria are better equipped to conserve the bronzes than those in Europe.
items.note: The writer discusses the objection about conservation and says it should be taken seriously, but makes no comparison between Nigerian and European museums.

items.stem: What does the writer say about the recent change in attitudes towards restitution?
options: It has been driven mainly by museum curators.
It has obliged museums to justify the purpose of their collections.
It began with Germany's decision to transfer the Benin Bronzes.
It has so far affected only national museums.
items.evidence: now find themselves obliged to defend not merely individual acquisitions but the very rationale of their collections
items.note: Curators are on the defensive, not leading the change (A); France acted before Germany (C); universities and smaller museums have also returned objects (D).

items.stem: In the fourth paragraph, the writer's comment about 'the values of the victorious party' suggests that
options: moral standards in the past were generally harsher than those of today.
the colonial powers disagreed among themselves about the expedition.
the opinions of those in power did not represent the views of everyone at the time.
the people of Benin City eventually accepted the loss of their treasures.
items.evidence: To treat the values of the victorious party as the values of the era is to mistake power for consensus.
items.note: B misreads 'deplored by some observers'; D contradicts 'did not consent to it'.

items.stem: According to the writer, the case of the Parthenon sculptures is particularly difficult because
options: it turns on whether their removal was lawful rather than on the use of force.
the British Museum has refused to consider any kind of arrangement.
Greece has only recently begun to ask for their return.
the Ottoman authorities later denied giving Elgin permission.
items.evidence: how much more intractable the issue becomes when legality, rather than outright violence, is in dispute
items.note: The museum has floated a loan (B); Greece has sought their return since the 1980s (C); the text says the document is missing, not that permission was denied (D).

items.stem: What is the writer's main conclusion?
options: Museums should return every object that was acquired abroad.
Digital copies offer a workable compromise between the two sides.
Most disputes can be resolved simply by transferring ownership.
Where coercion is proven, museums should have to justify keeping an object.
items.evidence: the burden of proof should rest with the institution that wishes to retain an object rather than with those who want it back
items.note: A and C are explicitly rejected in the opening sentence of the paragraph, and B is rejected in 'Nor are digital replicas ... an adequate substitute'.
